newsitem.title: CANADA: FORECAST - Canadian economy seen spurting ahead.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Canadian economy seen spurting ahead.

text.p: A strong shot of economic growth mixed in with low inflation during the next two years will help Canada shed its reputation as the anemic child of the G7 nations, according to economists in a Reuters poll.

The first Reuters quarterly Canadian survey asked 24 economists in Canada and the United States to forecast key economic indicators for the next eight quarters. Some experts opted to forecast only certain items.
The consensus is that the Canadian economy, sluggish for two years, will grow robustly in a number of key areas.

Twenty-three economists in Canada and the United States predicted, on average, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth would pick up significantly to 3.2 percent in the current quarter from 0.3 percent in the second quarter of 1996.

That pace will continue through the end of 1997 with GDP growth fluctuating in a 2.5-3.0 percent range. Only in the second quarter of 1998 will growth ebb below the 2.0 percent mark, the economists forecast.

On the inflation front, consumers can expect to pay a bit more at the retail tills later this year as the Consumer Price Index (CPI) jumps to 1.6 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996. The latest government statistics show inflation running at an almost negligible 0.1 percent for August 1996.
The CPI, which exludes food and energy prices, will plateau at about 1.9 percent by the beginning of 1998, the economists estimated.
Survey participants said recent moves to lower interest rates will jump start Canada's economic engine.

"Monetary policy is sufficiently stimulative right now that it will provide a good boost to the economy and offset ongoing fiscal restraint," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at the Bank of Montreal.

The Bank of Canada has lowered its key bank rate nine times this year and by a total of 450 basis points since May 1995. The bank rate, currently 3.75 percent, is the top of the central bank's target range for overnight lending to financial institutions.

It determines prime lending rates by the commercial banks, which are currently at 5.25 percent -- the lowest level since 1959. Many economists believe rates will move even lower in the coming months, providing further stimulus to growth.
If that projected growth materializes, Canadians can expect an easing of the unemployment rate, according to the survey. Every economist polled predicted a drop in the nation's jobless numbers.

Canada's unemployment rate stands at 9.9 percent, more than 4.0 percent greater than the corresponding figure in the United States. Last week, Canada's Liberal government took heat from opposition politicians for failing to create sufficient jobs by maintaining an austere fiscal policy and exceeding its budget deficit-cutting targets.

Ferley was the most bullish on his unemployment projection, predicting a 1.2 percentage point drop in the jobless rate by the first quarter of 1998. He said continued slack in the economy would not offset an increase in new jobs.
However, some economists are warning Canadians not to pop the champagne just yet.
Don McIver, chief economist at Sun Life Assurance Co of Canada, has some equivocation about the rosy economic scenario painted by other economists.
"It is so strongly based on the export side of the economy which could come crashing down if the U.S. economy starts slowing," McIver cautioned.
Canada's dependency on international markets, mainly the United States, may come unhinged with a sudden appreciation in the value of the Canadian dollar, McIver said.
The survey projects that the average value of the Canadian dollar will hit C$1.3266 (US$0.7538) by the third quarter of 1998. The exchange rate is now around C$1.3525 (US$0.7394).
Despite moves by the Bank of Canada to lubricate the economy, growth north of the 49th parallel has yet to match the strong economic recovery in the United States.
McIver said he doubts that the central bank can continue to use monetary policy as its main tool to spur economic growth.
-- Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8100
